chapter: 3 Introduction to TensorFlow, PyTorch, JAX, and Keras

questions.question: Which three frameworks does chapter 3 introduce as usable with Keras?
questions.answer: TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX.
questions.explanation: They are listed on the opening page with their URLs.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT one of the stated goals of chapter 3?
options: Training a convnet for image classification
A closer look at the major deep learning frameworks and their relationships
How core deep learning concepts translate to code across frameworks
Reviewing core neural network components as Keras APIs
questions.answer: Training a convnet for image classification
questions.explanation: The other three appear in the chapter-covers box and the introduction. Real-world applications start in chapter 4; convnets come later still.

questions.question: Before reading on, can you name the components of a training setup from chapter 2 that you expect to see as Keras APIs (e.g. layers, model, loss, optimizer, training loop)?
questions.answer: Layers (Dense), a model chaining them, a loss, an optimizer, the fit loop, evaluation and prediction.
questions.explanation: Section 3.6 covers layers, models, compile (loss, optimizer, metrics), fit, validation and inference, mirroring the from-scratch pieces of pp.77-82.

questions.question: Why might it help to learn TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX if you will mostly write Keras code?
questions.answer: Because Keras runs on top of them; understanding the backend clarifies what Keras does underneath, lets you read code written directly in those frameworks, and helps you choose a backend.
questions.explanation: The chapter frames the frameworks as things that 'can be used with Keras', and chapter 2 already relied on TensorFlow's autodiff (p.80). The benefits listed are an inference from that framing.

questions.question: In which chapter does the book say practical, real-world applications begin?
questions.answer: Chapter 4.
questions.explanation: The last sentence of the page says so.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three key features the book says all deep learning frameworks combine?
options: Automatic differentiation of arbitrary differentiable functions
Running tensor computations on CPUs and GPUs
Distributing computation across multiple devices or computers
questions.answer: A library of pretrained models
questions.explanation: The three listed features are autodiff, CPU/GPU tensor computation and distribution. Pretrained model collections exist in many ecosystems but are not part of the book's definition.

questions.question: Which of the four frameworks covered in the book is the oldest, and when was it launched?
questions.answer: Keras, launched in March 2015.
questions.explanation: Stated in the second paragraph of section 3.1.

questions.question: According to the book, which was the first framework to enable both autodifferentiation and GPU computation for training deep learning models?
questions.answer: Theano
questions.explanation: Theano, circa 2009, is called the conceptual ancestor of all modern deep learning tools. Caffe was a C++ computer-vision library (p.86), TensorFlow came in late 2015, and CUDA is a GPU programming platform, not a deep learning framework.

questions.question: Automatic differentiation was described in 1964, yet it had no practical ML application until the 2000s. Using the page, explain what else was missing.
questions.answer: Practical GPU programming (CUDA only arrived in 2006), a convenient scientific language ecosystem (Python's rise in the late 2000s), and a reusable package combining autodiff with GPU computation (Theano, circa 2009). Demand also grew only after ImageNet 2012.
questions.explanation: The page emphasizes that the field had to develop robust solutions to all three problems and package them reusably; the idea alone was not enough.

questions.question: How did people working with neural networks compute gradients before frameworks?
questions.answer: They wrote their own gradient logic by hand, usually in a language like C++.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the history paragraph.

questions.question: Why does the third feature (distribution across devices and computers) matter for modern deep learning?
questions.answer: Large models and datasets exceed the memory and compute of one device, so training must be split across several GPUs in one machine or across multiple machines.
questions.explanation: The page lists distribution as one of the three features that unlock modern deep learning; the reasoning about scale is an elaboration beyond the page.

questions.question: Can you place these on a timeline without looking: CUDA, Theano, ImageNet 2012, Keras, the first autodiff paper?
questions.answer: Autodiff paper 1964; CUDA 2006; Theano circa 2009; ImageNet 2012; Keras March 2015.
questions.explanation: All dates are on this page.

questions.question: Which library powered Keras when it launched in early 2015?
questions.answer: Theano
questions.explanation: Keras launched as a higher-level library powered by Theano. TensorFlow came in late 2015, PyTorch about a year after that, and JAX a few years later.

questions.question: Which two earlier projects did PyTorch take ideas from?
questions.answer: Chainer and NumPy-Autograd.
questions.explanation: Chainer was a niche but innovative framework from mid-2015; NumPy-Autograd was a 2014 CPU-only autodiff library for NumPy by Maclaurin et al.

questions.question: What was XLA originally developed for, according to the page?
options: To enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs
To run Lua code on GPUs
questions.answer: To enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs
questions.explanation: XLA is described as a high-performance compiler developed to enable TensorFlow to run on TPUs; JAX later used it. Autodiff for NumPy was NumPy-Autograd; Lua was Torch 7; nothing on the page ties XLA to PyTorch.

questions.question: Why do the authors consider using Keras a considerable advantage in a multiframework world?
questions.answer: Because Keras models can run on any backend, including future frameworks via a new Keras backend, so your models are not locked into one framework's fate; Keras has provided this stability since 2015.
questions.explanation: This is the argument of the second 'certainty' bullet, supported by the history of Keras moving from Theano to TensorFlow and beyond.

questions.question: What fact does the page give about Keras usage among TensorFlow users by mid-2016?
questions.answer: Over half of all TensorFlow users were using it through Keras.
questions.explanation: Stated in the TensorFlow paragraph.

questions.question: Why do the authors think new hardware is unlikely to disrupt your workflows?
questions.answer: Any new chip will have to work with the existing frameworks to gain traction, so code written against those frameworks keeps working.
questions.explanation: Frameworks act as the abstraction layer between models and hardware; the third bullet argues hardware adapts to them.

questions.question: Can you separate the page's historical claims from its predictions? List two of each.
questions.answer: Historical: TensorFlow launched in late 2015 with distributed computation; JAX was released by Matthew Johnson at Google. Predictions: Python will not be replaced in the next 15 years; new chips will have to work with existing frameworks.
questions.explanation: The shift is signalled by 'If you ask me, three things today are certain'.

questions.question: In the book's house-building analogy, what does Keras correspond to?
options: The land the house is built on
questions.answer: A prefabricated building kit
questions.explanation: Keras provides a streamlined interface for setting up and training networks, like a prefab kit. TensorFlow, PyTorch and JAX are the raw materials. The other two options are not in the analogy.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to the low-level tensor manipulation layer rather than to the high-level Keras concepts?
questions.answer: Backpropagation
questions.explanation: The page lists tensors/variables, tensor operations and backpropagation as low-level; optimizer, metrics and training loop are high-level Keras concepts.

questions.question: Why can Keras running on the NumPy backend make predictions but not train a model?
questions.answer: NumPy provides no API for gradients, and training requires computing gradients of the loss with respect to the weights.
questions.explanation: Prediction needs only the forward computation; training needs automatic differentiation, which NumPy lacks.

questions.question: Map each piece of the chapter 2 from-scratch code to the page's concept lists: keras.Variable, ops.matmul, tf.GradientTape, NaiveSequential, update_weights, fit().
questions.answer: keras.Variable: tensors/variables (low). ops.matmul: tensor operations (low). tf.GradientTape: backpropagation (low). NaiveSequential: layers combined into a model (high). update_weights: optimizer (high). fit(): training loop (high).
questions.explanation: The page says training revolves around these concepts 'as you saw in the previous chapters'; the from-scratch code implemented each one explicitly.

questions.question: Why does footnote 2 call PyTorch an intermediate case?
questions.answer: Because, although mainly low level, it includes its own layers and optimizers; with Keras, though, you only use its low-level APIs.
questions.explanation: Direct from footnote 2.

questions.question: Give TensorFlow's initial, v1 and v2 release dates.
questions.answer: Initial release November 2015; v1 February 2017; v2 October 2019.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of section 3.3.

questions.question: Can you explain to someone why 'Should I learn Keras or TensorFlow?' is a slightly malformed question?
questions.answer: They are at different levels: Keras is a high-level API that runs on top of a low-level backend like TensorFlow (or PyTorch or JAX), so you typically use both together.
questions.explanation: This is the central point of section 3.2.

questions.question: Which TensorFlow ecosystem component does the page associate with model quantization and pruning?
questions.answer: TF Optimization Toolkit
questions.explanation: The page lists the TF Optimization Toolkit for quantization and pruning. TFX is for ML workflow management, TF-Serving for production deployment, and MediaPipe (with TFLite) for mobile deployment.

questions.question: What does tf.zeros(shape=(2, 1)) return, including shape and dtype?
questions.answer: tf.Tensor([[0.], [0.]], shape=(2, 1), dtype=float32)
questions.explanation: Listing 3.1 prints exactly this: a column of two zeros, float32 by default.

questions.question: Which NumPy call is equivalent to tf.constant([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32") according to the listing's callout?
questions.answer: np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")
questions.explanation: The callout says 'Equivalent to np.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")'. np.ones/np.zeros would fill with constants and np.random draws random values.

questions.question: Why do the four key concepts of 3.3.1 suffice to build a model trained by gradient descent?
questions.answer: Tensors and variables hold data and state, operations express the model and loss, GradientTape computes gradients of the loss with respect to the variables, and compilation makes the step fast; that is everything a gradient-descent training step needs.
questions.explanation: These match the low-level ingredients on p.87 (tensors, operations, backpropagation). p.93 confirms that knowing tensors, variables, operations and gradients is enough to build any gradient-descent model.

questions.question: What shape does tf.constant([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32") have, and what is its rank?
questions.answer: Shape (3,); rank 1.
questions.explanation: The printed output shows shape=(3,): one axis with three entries.

questions.question: Which submodule does the page name for creating tensors filled with random values?
questions.answer: tf.random
questions.explanation: The page says random tensors come from methods of tf.random, equivalent to np.random. tf.math holds operations, tf.data is the input pipeline API, and tf.init does not exist.

questions.question: Without running code, can you write the printed output of tf.ones(shape=(1, 3))?
questions.answer: tf.Tensor([[1., 1., 1.]], shape=(1, 3), dtype=float32)
questions.explanation: One outer entry containing three ones: a row vector. Compare with the (2, 1) column in Listing 3.1.

questions.question: What happens when you run x = tf.ones(shape=(2, 2)); x[0, 0] = 0.0?
options: A new tensor is returned and x is unchanged silently
An error: EagerTensor object does not support item assignment
x is converted to a tf.Variable automatically
questions.answer: An error: EagerTensor object does not support item assignment
questions.explanation: TensorFlow tensors are constant (Listing 3.4). The first option is the NumPy behavior (Listing 3.3); there is no silent copy and no automatic conversion to a variable.

questions.question: Give the NumPy equivalent of tf.random.uniform(shape=(3, 1), minval=0., maxval=1.).
questions.answer: np.random.uniform(size=(3, 1), low=0., high=1.)
questions.explanation: Stated in the callout next to Listing 3.2.

questions.question: Why does TensorFlow need a Variable class at all?
questions.answer: Training must update the model's state (its weights), but tensors are constant and cannot be modified; tf.Variable is the class for modifiable state.
questions.explanation: This is the reasoning in the paragraph before Listing 3.5.

questions.question: Which framework, according to the book, has tensors that ARE assignable like NumPy arrays?
questions.answer: PyTorch
questions.explanation: p.100 states PyTorch tensors are assignable, unlike TensorFlow's. JAX arrays (p.109) are not assignable, consistent with its stateless design.

questions.question: For tf.random.uniform(shape=(3, 1), minval=0., maxval=1.), what is the expected value of each entry, and what is the expected sum of the three entries?
questions.answer: 0.5 each; 1.5 for the sum.
questions.explanation: The mean of U(a, b) is (a+b)/2 = 0.5; by linearity the sum of three independent draws has expectation 1.5. (The book's sample sums to about 1.18.)

questions.question: What determines the shape and dtype of v in Listing 3.5?
questions.answer: The initial value: tf.random.normal(shape=(3, 1)), so shape (3, 1) and float32.
questions.explanation: A variable is created from an initial value, which fixes its shape and dtype.

questions.question: Can you explain, in one sentence each, the role of a tf.Tensor and of a tf.Variable in a training step?
questions.answer: Tensors carry intermediate values (inputs, activations, gradients) that are computed fresh each step; variables hold the weights that persist and are updated across steps.
questions.explanation: This restates the page's state-versus-value distinction in training terms.

questions.question: Which call updates only the first coefficient of the (3, 1) variable v to 3.0?
questions.answer: v[0, 0].assign(3.)
questions.explanation: Listing 3.7. Direct item assignment fails on TensorFlow objects; v.assign(3.) would try to replace the whole value; assign_add would add 3 to every entry.

questions.question: In Listing 3.9, what are e = tf.matmul(a, b) and the shape of f = tf.concat((a, b), axis=0)?
questions.explanation: b = a = all ones, so each entry of e is 1·1 + 1·1 = 2. Concatenating two (2, 2) tensors along axis 0 stacks rows: (4, 2).

questions.question: What are the NumPy equivalents of assign_add and assign_sub, according to the page?
questions.answer: += and -=
questions.explanation: The page calls them efficient equivalents of += and -=.

questions.question: Starting from v = [[3.], [1.], [1.]] (after Listing 3.7), what would v.assign_add(tf.ones((3, 1))) return?
questions.explanation: Element-wise addition of ones. The book's printed result [[2.], [2.], [2.]] corresponds to starting from all ones.

questions.question: Which TensorFlow function is the counterpart of np.concatenate?
questions.answer: tf.concat
questions.explanation: Listing 3.9's callout: 'Concatenates a and b along axis 0, same as np.concatenate'. tf.stack creates a new axis instead, tf.join is not a tensor op, and tf.matmul is the tensor product.

questions.question: How would you write a gradient-descent update of a weight variable W in TensorFlow using what this page introduces?
questions.answer: W.assign_sub(learning_rate * grad_W), i.e. compute the step with tensor ops and subtract it in place.
questions.explanation: assign_sub is the in-place -=; the update W ← W − η·∇W is exactly that. This is how the TensorFlow training step later works (p.93 onward).

questions.question: Can you predict d = b + c in Listing 3.9 if a were tf.fill((2, 2), 4.) instead of ones?
questions.answer: b = 16, c = 2 element-wise, so d is a 2x2 tensor of 18s.
questions.explanation: Square of 4 is 16 and its square root is 2; addition is element-wise.

questions.question: What value does gradient hold at the end of Listing 3.10?
questions.explanation: result = x² with x = 3; d(x²)/dx = 2x = 6.

questions.question: Why is tape.watch(input_const) needed in Listing 3.11?
options: Because tf.square only works on watched tensors
Because only trainable variables are tracked by default, and input_const is a constant
Because constants cannot be differentiated at all
Because the tape must be told the output tensor
questions.answer: Because only trainable variables are tracked by default, and input_const is a constant
questions.explanation: The page says constants must be manually marked. tf.square works on any tensor; constants can be differentiated once watched; and the target is passed to tape.gradient, not watched.

questions.question: Why doesn't the tape record the information needed to differentiate everything with respect to everything?
questions.answer: It would be too expensive (memory and compute) to store that information preemptively; so the tape only watches what it is told to, with trainable variables watched by default as the most common case.
questions.explanation: Direct paraphrase of the paragraph after Listing 3.11.

questions.question: Write the dense function given on the page.
questions.answer: def dense(inputs, W, b): return tf.nn.relu(tf.matmul(inputs, W) + b)
questions.explanation: It is the TensorFlow equivalent of chapter 2's Dense layer.

questions.question: What is the most common use of the gradient tape according to the page?
options: Computing gradients of a model's loss with respect to its weights
questions.answer: Computing gradients of a model's loss with respect to its weights
questions.explanation: gradients = tape.gradient(loss, weights). Second-order gradients are possible but less common; compilation is tf.function; watching constants is a special case.

questions.question: If Listing 3.10 used initial_value=-2.0 and result = tf.square(input_var) * 5, what would the gradient be?
Can you explain, without looking, what would go wrong if you computed result outside the with tf.GradientTape() block?
questions.answer: The operation would not be recorded on the tape, so the tape would have no path from input to result and could not return a gradient (it returns None).
questions.explanation: The tape only knows about operations executed inside its scope (the None return value is a detail beyond the book).

questions.question: For position(time) = 4.9 * time ** 2, what do speed and acceleration equal at time = 0.0 in Listing 3.12?
questions.answer: speed = 0.0, acceleration = 9.8
questions.explanation: speed = 9.8·time = 0 at t = 0; acceleration = 9.8 for all t (the callout: 4.9 * 2 = 9.8).

questions.question: Why is speed computed inside the outer tape's with block in Listing 3.12?
options: Because the inner tape is closed after that line
So that the outer tape records the computation of speed and can differentiate it
Because tf.Variable can only be used inside a tape
questions.answer: So that the outer tape records the computation of speed and can differentiate it
questions.explanation: The outer tape can only differentiate what it recorded. Variables work anywhere; speed of execution is irrelevant; the inner tape's closing is not the reason.

questions.question: What is operation fusion? Give the page's example.
questions.answer: Replacing consecutive operations with a single, more efficient one that doesn't materialize the intermediate output, e.g. matmul followed by relu.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph on eager execution.

questions.question: What drawback of compilation do the authors mention?
options: The code you write is no longer the code that gets executed, making debugging painful
questions.answer: The code you write is no longer the code that gets executed, making debugging painful
questions.explanation: That is the stated drawback. Results are the same, compilation is not GPU-only, and only the first call is slower.

questions.question: Why is the first call to a @tf.function-decorated dense slower than the following calls?
questions.answer: On the first call TensorFlow compiles the function into an optimized program; this happens once, and later calls reuse the compiled program.
questions.explanation: Paraphrase of p092_e11.

questions.question: If position(time) = 2 * time ** 3, what would Listing 3.12's acceleration be at time = 1.0?
questions.explanation: speed = 6t², acceleration = 12t = 12 at t = 1.

questions.question: Can you describe the workflow the authors recommend for using compilation?
questions.answer: Write and debug the code eagerly in the Python runtime first; only then turn on compilation with @tf.function for speed.
questions.explanation: Recommendation from the paragraph on compilation's drawback.

questions.question: How do you enable XLA compilation for a TensorFlow function?
questions.answer: @tf.function(jit_compile=True)
questions.explanation: Shown on the page. Plain @tf.function gives graph mode; @tf.xla is not the API; run_functions_eagerly disables compilation.

questions.question: What does XLA stand for, and what trade-off does it have versus graph mode?
questions.answer: Accelerated Linear Algebra; often faster than graph mode, but the first execution takes longer because the compiler does more work.
questions.explanation: Both stated on the page.

questions.question: According to the callouts, what do the mean and the covariance matrix describe about each point cloud?
questions.answer: The mean describes its position in the plane; the covariance matrix describes its shape.
questions.explanation: The two classes have different positions (means) and the same shape (covariance).

questions.question: What shape does negative_samples have?
questions.explanation: 1,000 samples of 2D points (confirmed on p.94). (2000, 2) is the stacked array built next; the others transpose or drop an axis.

questions.question: What is the Euclidean distance between the two class means, and what is the correlation between the two coordinates within a class?
questions.answer: Distance √(3² + 3²) = 3√2 ≈ 4.24; correlation 0.5 / √(1 × 1) = 0.5.
questions.explanation: Means (0, 3) and (3, 0); covariance 0.5 with unit variances.

questions.question: Why is this dataset well suited to a linear classifier?
questions.answer: It is designed to be linearly separable: two compact clouds with the same shape, centered far apart, so a straight line divides them.
questions.explanation: The authors call it 'nicely linearly separable synthetic data'.

questions.question: Can you list the ingredients you'll need from 3.3.1 to train this classifier, and which TensorFlow API provides each?
questions.answer: Parameters W and b as tf.Variable; forward pass and loss with ops like tf.matmul; gradients with tf.GradientTape; updates with assign_sub; optionally speed with @tf.function.
questions.explanation: These are exactly the pieces the page says suffice for any gradient-descent model.

questions.question: What is the shape of `np.vstack((negative_samples, positive_samples))` when both arrays have shape (1000, 2)?
questions.explanation: `vstack` concatenates along the rows (axis 0), so the row counts add up and the column count stays 2. (1000, 4) would be `hstack` (columns concatenated), (2, 1000, 2) would be `np.stack` (new leading axis), and (1000, 2, 2) would be stacking along a new last axis.

questions.question: Why does listing 3.14 call `.astype(np.float32)`?
questions.answer: Because `np.random.multivariate_normal` returns float64 data, while the TensorFlow model variables and operations in this example are float32; the cast makes the dtypes compatible.
questions.explanation: TensorFlow does not implicitly mix float64 and float32 in ops like `tf.matmul`; float32 is also the standard deep-learning precision (TensorFlow tensors default to float32, p.88).

questions.question: What would go wrong if listing 3.15 stacked the ones before the zeros, while listing 3.14 kept negatives first?
questions.answer: Every label would be flipped: class-0 points would be labeled 1 and vice versa.
questions.explanation: The correspondence between inputs and targets is purely positional: `targets[i, 0]` describes `inputs[i]`. Flipping the order of one but not the other inverts all labels. The model would still learn a line, but it would predict the opposite class names, which is a silent bug.

questions.question: The targets have shape (2000, 1) rather than (2000,). What could happen in the loss computation `targets - predictions` if they were (2000,) while predictions are (2000, 1)?
questions.answer: Broadcasting would produce a (2000, 2000) matrix of differences, so the mean squared error would be computed over all pairs of samples instead of matching pairs, without raising an error.
questions.explanation: Broadcasting aligns trailing axes: (2000,) is treated as (1, 2000) and (2000, 1) is expanded across columns, giving (2000, 2000). Matching shapes, as the book chooses, avoid this.

questions.question: In listing 3.16, what does `inputs[:, 1]` select?
options: The y coordinates of all samples
questions.answer: The y coordinates of all samples
questions.explanation: `:` on axis 0 keeps every row, `1` on axis 1 picks the second column, which holds the y coordinate of each point. The second sample would be `inputs[1]`; labels live in `targets`; the first 1,000 samples would be `inputs[:1000]`.

questions.question: Looking at figure 3.1, roughly where are the two classes centered, and what in listing 3.13 determines that?
questions.answer: One class (dark) is centered near (0, 3) and the other (yellow) near (3, 0); these are the `mean` arguments passed to `np.random.multivariate_normal` on p.93.
questions.explanation: The scatter plot is a direct picture of the sampling distributions; the shared covariance `[[1, 0.5], [0.5, 1]]` explains the tilted, elongated shape of both clouds.

questions.question: Without looking, write the three listings on this page from memory, then check the shapes of `inputs` and `targets` by printing `.shape` and `.dtype`.
questions.answer: inputs: (2000, 2) float32; targets: (2000, 1) float32.
questions.explanation: Being able to prepare and sanity-check aligned input/target arrays is the prerequisite for every training loop in the book, starting with the one on pp.95-96.

questions.question: What are the shapes of W and b in listing 3.17?
questions.explanation: W is created with `shape=(input_dim, output_dim)` = (2, 1) and b with `shape=(output_dim,)` = (1,). (1, 2) would not multiply with (2000, 2) inputs on the right; (2, 2) would give two outputs; (2000, 2) is the shape of the data, not of the parameters.

questions.question: With w1 = 0.2, w2 = -0.1 and b = 0.4, what is the prediction for the point [x, y] = [3, 1]? Which class does it get with a 0.5 threshold?
questions.explanation: Use prediction = w1 * x + w2 * y + b from p.95, and the 0.5 threshold described on p.96.

questions.question: Targets are [0, 1, 1] and predictions are [0.3, 0.9, 0.5]. What does `mean_squared_error` return?
questions.explanation: Squared differences: (0 - 0.3)^2 = 0.09, (1 - 0.9)^2 = 0.01, (1 - 0.5)^2 = 0.25; reduce_mean averages them.

questions.question: Why does `mean_squared_error` end with `tf.reduce_mean` instead of returning `per_sample_losses` directly?
questions.answer: Gradient descent needs a single scalar loss to differentiate; reduce_mean averages the per-sample scores into one value.
questions.explanation: The callout on listing 3.19 says exactly this. Averaging (rather than summing) also keeps the loss scale independent of the number of samples, so the learning rate does not have to change with dataset size.

questions.question: Why are W and b created as `tf.Variable` rather than as constant tensors?
options: TensorFlow tensors are immutable, and the training step must update W and b in place
questions.answer: TensorFlow tensors are immutable, and the training step must update W and b in place
questions.explanation: Variables hold mutable state, updated with assign_sub on p.96. Speed, dtype and tf.matmul's accepted arguments have nothing to do with it: constants can be float32 and tf.matmul accepts any tensor.

questions.question: What is the role of `b` geometrically, and why is it called an affine (not linear) transformation?
questions.answer: b shifts the output by a constant, which lets the decision line w1 * x + w2 * y + b = 0.5 be placed anywhere in the plane; a map with an added constant is affine, while a strictly linear map must send 0 to 0.
questions.explanation: Without b, the prediction at the origin would always be 0, constraining where the boundary can lie.

questions.question: Can you rewrite listings 3.17-3.19 from memory and state the shape of every tensor involved (inputs, W, b, predictions, per_sample_losses, loss)?
questions.answer: inputs (2000, 2); W (2, 1); b (1,); predictions (2000, 1); per_sample_losses (2000, 1); loss () scalar.
questions.explanation: The authors say that this time you should understand every line; tracing shapes is the quickest way to check that you do.

questions.question: What does `W.assign_sub(grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate)` do?
options: Creates a new tensor W - grad * lr and returns it
Subtracts grad * lr from the variable W in place
Resets W to its initial value
questions.answer: Subtracts grad * lr from the variable W in place
questions.explanation: assign_sub is the in-place `-=` of a tf.Variable, which is exactly the gradient-descent update. It does not create a new tensor (that would be W - x), does not add (assign_add), and has nothing to do with reinitialization.

questions.question: According to the authors, why does batch training justify a larger learning rate than mini-batch training?
questions.answer: Because each update uses information from all training samples, it is much more effective at reducing the training loss, so fewer, larger steps can be taken.
questions.explanation: The page contrasts 2,000 samples per update with, say, 128 random samples; beyond the book, a mini-batch gradient is a noisy estimate, which calls for smaller steps.

questions.question: Suppose at some step the gradient of the loss with respect to b is 0.3 and b = 0.2. With learning_rate = 0.1, what is b after the update?
questions.explanation: b.assign_sub(grad_loss_wrt_b * learning_rate) subtracts 0.03.

questions.question: What would happen if the line `predictions = model(inputs, W, b)` were moved above the `with tf.GradientTape() as tape:` line?
questions.answer: The tape would only record the loss computation from already-computed predictions, not the dependence on W and b, so tape.gradient would return None for W and b.
questions.explanation: The tape can only differentiate operations it recorded; the matmul with W and the add with b would have happened before recording started.

questions.question: In the final snippet, what does `c=predictions[:, 0] > 0.5` color the points by?
questions.answer: The model's predicted class
questions.explanation: The comparison yields True/False per point, i.e. predicted class 1 or 0. The true labels were used in listing 3.16; raw scores would be `predictions[:, 0]` without the comparison; per-sample losses are never plotted.

questions.question: Listing 3.20 calls `mean_squared_error(predictions, targets)`, but the function on p.95 is defined as `mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)`. Does this change the result? Why?
questions.answer: No. The function computes the square of the difference, and (a - b)^2 = (b - a)^2, so swapping the arguments gives the same loss and the same gradients.
questions.explanation: Argument order would matter for asymmetric losses like crossentropy, so it is a good habit to keep the (targets, predictions) order.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, what each of the four callouts in listing 3.20 points to, and how the loop in listing 3.21 relates to an epoch here?
questions.answer: tf.function decorator (speed); forward pass inside the tape scope; tape.gradient retrieving gradients of the loss with regard to the weights; assign_sub updating the weights. Each step uses the whole dataset, so each step is one epoch.
questions.explanation: Being able to narrate the training step is the goal the authors set on p.95: understand the code line by line.

questions.question: Derive the slope-intercept form of the boundary w1 * x + w2 * y + b = 0.5.
questions.explanation: Subtract w1 * x + b from both sides to get w2 * y = 0.5 - b - w1 * x, then divide by w2 (assuming w2 ≠ 0).

questions.question: With w1 = 0.2, w2 = -0.1 and b = 0.4, what are the slope and y-intercept of the decision line, and is class 1 above or below it?
questions.answer: Slope = -0.2 / -0.1 = 2; intercept = (0.5 - 0.4) / -0.1 = -1; so y = 2x - 1. Since w2 < 0, class 1 is below the line.
questions.explanation: Check with the point (3, 0), which is below y = 2x - 1 (at x = 3 the line is at 5): 0.2 * 3 + 0.4 = 1.0 > 0.5, so it is class 1.

questions.question: In the plotting snippet, what does the format string "-r" mean?
options: Plot red points without a line
questions.answer: Plot a red solid line
questions.explanation: The callout says '"-r" means plot it as a red line': '-' is the solid line style and 'r' the color red. It does not reverse data, draw markers only, or clear the figure.

questions.question: The text says 'Class 1 is above the line'. Looking at figure 3.3, is that what you see? Explain.
questions.answer: No: class 1 (yellow) is below/right of the red line. The 'above' statement holds when w2 > 0; dividing the inequality w1 * x + w2 * y + b > 0.5 by a negative w2 flips it, putting class 1 below the line.
questions.explanation: Class 1 is centered at (3, 0), below-right of class 0 at (0, 3), so the trained w2 is negative.

questions.question: Why are figures 3.2 and 3.1 'pretty similar' rather than identical?
questions.answer: Figure 3.2 shows predicted classes and figure 3.1 true classes; the blobs overlap slightly, so a few points near the boundary are misclassified by any straight line.
questions.explanation: A linear classifier can only draw a straight boundary; overlapping points on the wrong side get the wrong color.

questions.question: Which of these would change the position or orientation of the red line in figure 3.3?
questions.answer: Changing the threshold from 0.5 to 0.7
questions.explanation: The threshold enters the intercept (0.5 - b) / w2, so a different threshold shifts the line. The linspace range only changes how much of the same line is drawn; colors and plt.show() do not affect it.

questions.question: Could a linear classifier separate two classes arranged as a ring (class 1) around a central disk (class 0)? Explain using the decision-boundary view on this page.
questions.answer: No. Its boundary is always a straight line, and no line separates a disk from a surrounding ring.
questions.explanation: This limitation of linear models is the reason nonlinear, multilayer models are needed for harder problems.

questions.question: Which feature do the authors describe as unique to TensorFlow among all frameworks?
options: Support for string tensors and ragged tensors
questions.answer: Support for string tensors and ragged tensors
questions.explanation: The page says 'Unique among all frameworks, it has support for string tensors as well as ragged tensors'. Autodiff and GPU support are common to all three frameworks, and the NumPy-inconsistent API is listed as a flaw.

questions.question: What is a ragged tensor, and why is it useful?
questions.answer: A tensor whose entries may have different dimensions. It lets you handle sequences of different lengths without padding them to a shared length.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases the parenthetical definition on the page.

questions.question: The authors say TensorFlow's sprawling API is 'the flipside of being very feature complete.' Explain the trade-off.
questions.answer: Supporting nearly every need (strings, ragged data, preprocessing, deployment) requires thousands of operations. That breadth makes the API larger, more varied and harder to learn and navigate.
questions.explanation: The same property, breadth, appears as both a benefit and a flaw.

questions.question: From which framework does PyTorch inherit its programming style?
questions.answer: Chainer
questions.explanation: The page says PyTorch inherits its style from the now-defunct Chainer framework, which was inspired by NumPy-Autograd. PyTorch was released as a response to TensorFlow, not modeled on it, and Theano and Caffe aren't mentioned here.

questions.question: Give the release timeline of PyTorch stated on the page.
questions.answer: Original release in September 2016, version 1.0 in 2018 and version 2.0 in 2023.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in section 3.4's first paragraph.

questions.question: You need to deploy a model inside a mobile app and a web page. Based on this page, which framework's ecosystem is the strongest fit, and why?
questions.answer: TensorFlow, because its production-deployment ecosystem is the most mature among all frameworks, especially for mobile and the browser.
questions.explanation: This is the third benefit listed on the page.

questions.question: A trained linear classifier has w1 = 2, w2 = 1, b = −0.5. Write its decision line in the form y = a·x + c and classify the point (0.5, 0.5).
questions.answer: y = −2x + 1. For (0.5, 0.5): 2·0.5 + 0.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 > 0.5, so it is class 1 (above the line, since the line's y at x = 0.5 is 0).

questions.question: For your own projects, which of TensorFlow's listed benefits and flaws would matter most? Would they push you toward or away from TensorFlow as a Keras backend?
questions.answer: Open-ended. For example, deployment-heavy work favors TensorFlow, while work reusing the latest Hugging Face generative models favors PyTorch.
questions.explanation: The page frames the question 'When should you use TensorFlow, and when could you use something else?'

questions.question: Which call creates a 2×1 float32 tensor of ones in PyTorch, following the book's conventions?
questions.answer: torch.ones(size=(2, 1))
questions.explanation: The argument is named size, the package is torch, and dtype strings are not accepted. torch.ones already defaults to float32.

questions.question: How do you pass a dtype to torch.tensor, and what goes wrong with dtype="float32"?
questions.answer: Pass a torch dtype instance such as dtype=torch.float32. A string like "float32" is not accepted.
questions.explanation: From the second callout on Listing 3.22.

questions.question: In what sense is PyTorch's API 'higher level' than TensorFlow's and JAX's, according to the page?
questions.answer: It includes layers and optimizers, like Keras, rather than only low-level tensor operations and gradients. These are compatible with Keras workflows on the PyTorch backend.
questions.explanation: Stated in the page's first paragraph.

questions.question: How does torch.normal determine the shape of its output?
options: From the shape of the mean and standard deviation tensors passed to it
questions.answer: From the shape of the mean and standard deviation tensors passed to it
questions.explanation: The page says normal doesn't take a shape argument; the mean and std are provided as tensors with the expected output shape. There is no size argument in this usage, and it doesn't return only scalars.

questions.question: List the five key concepts that 3.4.1 promises to cover.
questions.answer: Tensors and parameters; numerical operations; computing gradients with backward(); packaging computation with the Module class; speeding up PyTorch with compilation.
questions.explanation: The bullet list on the page.

questions.question: Which chapter-2 idea does the backward() method implement?
questions.answer: Backpropagation, i.e. reverse-mode automatic differentiation: applying the chain rule to the computation graph from the loss back to the parameters.
questions.explanation: p.74 defines backprop and says frameworks such as PyTorch implement automatic differentiation; p.103 shows loss.backward() filling .grad.

questions.question: Rewrite Listing 3.22 in NumPy and TensorFlow from memory, then list every argument name or value that changes between the three versions.
questions.answer: The shape keyword vs size, the string dtype "float32" vs torch.float32, and the module names np, tf and torch.
questions.explanation: Writing all three makes the API differences pointed out on this page stick.

questions.question: Which call creates a (3, 1) tensor of uniform random values in [0, 1) in PyTorch, as shown on the page?
questions.answer: torch.rand(3, 1)
questions.explanation: The page states that `torch.rand` takes the output shape as independent arguments per dimension. `shape=` is TensorFlow's spelling, `torch.uniform(size=...)` mimics NumPy and is not what the book shows, and `torch.normal` draws from a Gaussian.

questions.question: How does `torch.normal` know the output shape in Listing 3.23?
questions.answer: From the shape of the `mean` and `std` tensors, both (3, 1).
questions.explanation: As the text explains, normal doesn't take a shape argument; mean and std are provided as tensors with the expected output shape.

questions.question: Why does PyTorch need a Parameter class even though its tensors are already assignable, whereas TensorFlow's equivalent role is played by tf.Variable?
questions.answer: Because in PyTorch mutability doesn't distinguish weights from other tensors, a dedicated type is needed to mark trainable state; this gives semantic clarity and lets PyTorch automatically track and retrieve Parameters in models. In TensorFlow, the only mutable class, tf.Variable, naturally plays that role.
questions.explanation: The book gives semantic clarity and automatic tracking as Parameter's benefits (p.100) and introduces tf.Variable as the class for modifiable state (p.89). The contrast in reasoning is an inference.

questions.question: What happens if you run `x = torch.zeros(size=(2, 1)); x[0, 0] = 1.`?
options: A new tensor is returned and x is unchanged
questions.answer: x becomes tensor([[1.], [0.]])
questions.explanation: PyTorch tensors are assignable; only element [0, 0] is changed in place. The error is what TensorFlow would raise; no copy is made; only one element is set.

questions.question: According to the callout on Listing 3.24, what kind of value can a Parameter be created from?
questions.answer: Only a torch.Tensor value — no NumPy arrays.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the callout next to `torch.nn.parameter.Parameter(data=x)`.

questions.question: Which Keras concept does the page compare PyTorch's Parameter to?
questions.answer: Keras Variable
questions.explanation: The page says automatic tracking of Parameters is similar to what Keras does with Keras Variable instances. Layers and models hold variables; optimizers update them, but neither is the analogue of the state object itself.

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, the PyTorch, TensorFlow and NumPy calls for a (3, 1) standard-normal tensor, and explain how each specifies the shape?
questions.answer: torch.normal(mean=torch.zeros(size=(3, 1)), std=torch.ones(size=(3, 1))); tf.random.normal(shape=(3, 1), mean=0., stddev=1.); np.random.normal(size=(3, 1), loc=0., scale=1.).
questions.explanation: PyTorch infers shape from the mean/std tensors, TensorFlow uses `shape=`, NumPy uses `size=` (p.88, p.100).

questions.question: In Listing 3.26, what value would input_var.grad hold if input_var were 5.0 instead of 3.0 (single backward call)?
questions.explanation: d(x²)/dx = 2x, so at x = 5 the gradient is 10.

questions.question: What is required for PyTorch to compute a gradient with respect to a tensor?
options: Wrapping the computation in a GradientTape
questions.answer: Creating the tensor with requires_grad=True
questions.explanation: Listing 3.26's callout says so. GradientTape is TensorFlow; compilation is unrelated to gradient tracking; NumPy arrays are not tracked at all.

questions.question: What is the shape of f = torch.cat((a, b), dim=0) in Listing 3.25?
questions.explanation: a and b are (2, 2); concatenating along axis 0 stacks rows: 2 + 2 = 4 rows of 2 columns.

questions.question: How does PyTorch's gradient mechanism differ from TensorFlow's GradientTape, according to the page?
questions.answer: There is no explicit tape object. PyTorch automatically creates a hidden one-time computation graph for every computation; you call backward() on the resulting tensor, and the gradients are written into the .grad attributes of tensors that track gradients.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases p101_e10; TensorFlow's tape is an explicit Python scope (p.80).

questions.question: You call result.backward() twice (rebuilding result each time) without resetting. What happens to .grad?
options: It holds the latest gradient only
It holds the sum of both gradients
questions.answer: It holds the sum of both gradients
questions.explanation: The page says each new call sums the new gradient with the preexisting one. Overwriting would be TensorFlow-like semantics; resetting to None is something you must do yourself (p.102).

questions.question: With a = torch.ones((2, 2)), what is every entry of e = torch.matmul(a, torch.square(a))?
questions.explanation: square(a) is all ones; each entry of the product is a dot product of a row and a column of ones: 1·1 + 1·1 = 2.

questions.question: Without looking, can you write the four lines needed to get the gradient of y = x² at x = 3 in PyTorch and state the expected output?
questions.answer: x = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True); y = torch.square(x); y.backward(); x.grad → tensor(6.)
questions.explanation: Matches Listing 3.26.

questions.question: input_var = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True). You run `torch.square(input_var).backward()` three times without resetting. What is input_var.grad?
questions.answer: tensor(18.)
questions.explanation: Each call adds 2·3 = 6, so 6 + 6 + 6 = 18. tensor(6.) would be correct only with a reset; 9 is x² itself, not a gradient; 216 = 6³ would imply multiplication rather than summation.

questions.question: How do you reset a tensor's accumulated gradient in the book's pure-PyTorch code?
questions.answer: Assign None to its .grad attribute, e.g. input_var.grad = None.
questions.explanation: The page states: 'To reset gradients, you can just set .grad to None'. The training step on p.103 does this for W and b.

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the only major difference between the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions of the linear classifier, and why do the variables need requires_grad=True?
questions.answer: How the gradients are computed. requires_grad=True makes PyTorch track operations on W and b so that backward() can populate W.grad and b.grad.
questions.explanation: TensorFlow asks a GradientTape for gradients; PyTorch uses loss.backward() and .grad. Without the flag, there is nothing to compute gradients with respect to.

questions.question: With inputs of shape (2000, 2), what are the shapes of W, b, model(inputs, W, b) and mean_squared_error(targets, predictions)?
questions.answer: W: (2, 1); b: (1,); predictions: (2000, 1); loss: scalar ().
questions.explanation: W = torch.rand(input_dim, output_dim) with input_dim = 2, output_dim = 1; b = torch.zeros(output_dim). (2000, 2)@(2, 1) = (2000, 1), the bias broadcasts, and torch.mean reduces to a scalar.

questions.question: Which PyTorch function replaces tf.reduce_mean in the loss function on this page?
questions.answer: torch.mean
questions.explanation: The book says 'from tf.reduce_mean to torch.mean'. torch.reduce_mean and torch.average do not exist in PyTorch; torch.sum would give the sum, not the mean, scaling the loss by N.

questions.question: Compute the MSE for targets (0, 1) and predictions (0.4, 0.6) as the page's mean_squared_error would.
questions.explanation: torch.square gives per-sample losses 0.16 and 0.16; torch.mean averages them.

questions.question: Can you explain, without looking, why a training loop that never resets .grad would behave badly?
questions.answer: Each step's update would use the sum of all gradients computed so far rather than the current gradient, so steps grow and point in stale directions, typically causing divergence.
questions.explanation: This follows from the accumulation rule shown on this page and is why step 4 on p.103 resets .grad and p.105 warns about forgetting model.zero_grad().

questions.question: Why are the updates of W and b done inside `torch.no_grad()`?
options: To make the update run on the GPU
Because the updates are not meant to be part of the backward pass, so gradient tracking is skipped
To reset W.grad and b.grad to zero
questions.answer: Because the updates are not meant to be part of the backward pass, so gradient tracking is skipped
questions.explanation: Point 3 says exactly this. no_grad has nothing to do with device placement, does not reset gradients (that is point 4) and computes nothing — backward() computes gradients.

questions.question: What would go wrong if the lines `W.grad = None` and `b.grad = None` were removed?
questions.answer: Gradients would accumulate across calls to training_step(), so each update would use the sum of all past gradients — invalid values.
questions.explanation: Point 4, building on the accumulation demo on p.102.

questions.question: What does `tensor.grad` represent after `loss.backward()`, and which tensors get it?
questions.answer: The gradient of the loss with regard to that tensor; it is populated on all tensors involved in computing the loss that track gradients (here W and b).
questions.explanation: Point 1. inputs and targets were not created with requires_grad=True, so they get no gradient.

questions.question: W = [[1.0], [0.0]], W.grad = [[0.5], [-2.0]], learning_rate = 0.1. What is W after the update?
In the Module API introduced on this page, where are the Parameters defined?
questions.answer: In __init__()
questions.explanation: The first bullet: hold some Parameters to store state variables, defined in __init__(). forward() implements the computation; the optimizer updates parameters but does not define them; backward() computes gradients.

questions.question: Which two classes does PyTorch's higher-level API rely on, and what is the Keras equivalent of torch.optim.SGD?
questions.answer: torch.nn.Module and an optimizer class from torch.optim (e.g. torch.optim.SGD); its Keras equivalent is keras.optimizers.SGD.
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph of 'Packaging state and computation with the Module class'.

questions.question: Can you write the full training step from memory, in the right order, and say what each line corresponds to in the TensorFlow version on p.96?
questions.answer: Forward + loss; loss.backward() (≈ tape.gradient); read W.grad/b.grad; update inside no_grad (≈ assign_sub); reset .grad (no TF equivalent); return loss.
questions.explanation: Comparing the two versions confirms the book's claim that the only major difference is how gradients are computed.

questions.question: Which line replaces `with torch.no_grad(): W -= grad_loss_wrt_W * learning_rate ...` in the simplified training step?
questions.answer: optimizer.step()
questions.explanation: The page says 'Now we can just do optimizer.step()'. backward() computes gradients, zero_grad() clears them, and model(inputs) is the forward pass.

questions.question: Why does the book call the model with `model(torch_inputs)` instead of `model.forward(torch_inputs)`?
questions.answer: Because __call__() redirects to forward() but also adds a few framework hooks.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after instantiation.

questions.question: How does the SGD optimizer know which tensors to update?
questions.answer: It is given them at construction: torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate); model.parameters() returns the registered Parameters W and b.
questions.explanation: The page states an optimizer needs the list of parameters it is intended to update, retrieved via .parameters().

questions.question: How many scalar values does model.parameters() contain for LinearModel with input_dim = 2 and output_dim = 1?
questions.answer: 3 (W has 2×1 = 2 entries, b has 1).
questions.explanation: W = Parameter(torch.rand(2, 1)), b = Parameter(torch.zeros(1)).

questions.question: Why does the simplified training_step take only (inputs, targets)?
options: Because W and b are no longer needed
Because the model object owns W and b as Parameters
Because the loss function stores W and b
questions.answer: Because the model object owns W and b as Parameters
questions.explanation: Listing 3.27 stores self.W and self.b on the Module. They are still needed; the optimizer updates existing tensors in place rather than creating new ones; the loss function holds no state.

questions.question: Map each line of the simplified step to the manual step on p.103.
questions.answer: model(inputs) ↔ model(inputs, W, b); loss line unchanged; loss.backward() unchanged; optimizer.step() ↔ the no_grad update; model.zero_grad() ↔ W.grad = None, b.grad = None.
questions.explanation: The page explicitly shows the old update replaced by optimizer.step(); p.105 explains zero_grad() replacing the manual resets.

questions.question: Could you rewrite LinearModel so input_dim and output_dim are constructor arguments, and still train it with the same training step?
questions.answer: Yes: def __init__(self, input_dim, output_dim): super().__init__(); self.W = ...; self.b = ...; then model = LinearModel(2, 1). The training step is unchanged.
questions.explanation: Checks understanding that the step depends only on the Module/optimizer interface, not on how the Parameters are created.

questions.question: Which call, according to the book, is a major (and common) bug to forget in a PyTorch training step?
questions.answer: model.zero_grad()
questions.explanation: The book explicitly warns not to forget model.zero_grad(). Forgetting backward() or step() would also break training, but visibly (no learning); forgetting zero_grad() silently accumulates gradients. torch.compile is optional.

questions.question: What does model.zero_grad() replace from the manual training step?
questions.answer: Setting tensor.grad = None on each parameter by hand (W.grad = None, b.grad = None).
questions.explanation: First paragraph of the page; compare p.103.

questions.question: What is the 'spooky action at a distance' the authors mention, and what really connects the loss, the optimizer and the Module?
questions.answer: The three objects seem aware of each other without being passed to one another. In fact they share references to the same parameter tensors: the Module registers them, the optimizer received them via model.parameters(), and the loss graph leads back to them, so backward() writes .grad that step() reads and zero_grad() clears.
questions.explanation: The book names the phenomenon; the mechanism is an AI explanation building on p.104's optimizer construction.

questions.question: What is the name of PyTorch's compiler used by torch.compile()?
questions.answer: Dynamo
questions.explanation: The page: 'This API uses PyTorch's very own compiler, named Dynamo.' XLA is TensorFlow/JAX's compiler; TorchScript is an older PyTorch mechanism not mentioned here; Inductor (beyond the book) is a backend Dynamo hands graphs to.

questions.question: Give the book's two reasons why most PyTorch code does not use compilation.
questions.answer: The compiler may not work with all models, and it may not give a speedup even when it does work.
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the decorator example; the authors add that PyTorch's compiler is relatively recent.

questions.question: TensorFlow and JAX also execute eagerly by default. Why, then, is eager execution presented as a PyTorch strength?
questions.answer: Because PyTorch is intended to run eagerly at all times, whereas serious TensorFlow or JAX projects inevitably need compilation, which significantly hurts debugging.
questions.explanation: First key strength in section 3.4.3.

questions.question: Can you write a PyTorch training step from memory, including the three-call incantation, and say what would happen if you swapped the order of step() and zero_grad()?
questions.answer: forward → loss → loss.backward() → optimizer.step() → model.zero_grad(). If zero_grad() came before step(), the gradients would be cleared before the update, so step() would do nothing (or skip parameters whose grad is None).
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of what each call reads and writes (the swap consequence is beyond the book).

questions.question: According to the authors, what is the primary drive behind PyTorch adoption today?
options: Hugging Face's first-class support for PyTorch
questions.answer: Hugging Face's first-class support for PyTorch
questions.explanation: Stated in the first bullet. The page says PyTorch is the slowest major framework, that its API is inconsistent with NumPy, and associates TPUs with JAX.

questions.question: Give the two examples the book uses to show PyTorch's API is internally inconsistent.
questions.answer: The keyword axis is sometimes named dim depending on the function; some pseudo-random number generation operations take a seed argument and others don't.
questions.explanation: From the first downside bullet.

questions.question: What speedups does the book say you may see with JAX compared to PyTorch?
questions.answer: 20% or 30% for most models; 3× or 5× for some, especially large, models — even after torch.compile().
questions.explanation: Second downside bullet.

questions.question: What does it mean that JAX is stateless, and why does that help with scale?
questions.answer: JAX functions keep no persistent state between calls (unlike imperative code where variables hold values). Because functions can execute independently without synchronization, computation can be parallelized and distributed automatically.
questions.explanation: Paraphrases the two paragraphs on statelessness.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT among the concepts listed for 3.5.1 on this page?
questions.answer: The Module class
questions.explanation: The Module class is PyTorch's (p.103). The other three are the listed JAX concepts on this page (gradients and JIT compilation follow on p.107).

questions.question: Contrast how W and b are handled in the PyTorch Module training step (p.104) with what statelessness implies for JAX.
questions.answer: In PyTorch, W and b are persistent attributes of the Module, updated in place by optimizer.step() and with gradients stored on them. In stateless JAX they must be passed into functions as arguments and their new values returned.
questions.explanation: Combines p.104 with this page's definition; p.112 confirms the JAX style.

questions.question: If you were starting a project fine-tuning a popular pretrained model versus training a very large model from scratch on TPUs, which framework would the arguments on this page point toward in each case?
questions.answer: Fine-tuning a popular pretrained model: PyTorch (Hugging Face availability). Very large training on TPUs: JAX (speed, TPU support, scalability from statelessness).
questions.explanation: Applies the authors' strengths and weaknesses to practical choices; this is an inference, not a recommendation stated on the page.

questions.question: What are the two minor differences between jax.numpy and the NumPy API named on this page?
options: Random number generation and array assignment
questions.answer: Random number generation and array assignment
questions.explanation: Stated right after Listing 3.28. Array creation, matmul, broadcasting and axis behave as in NumPy — that is the point of JAX implementing the NumPy API as is.

questions.question: Why does the second call to np.random.normal(size=(3,)) in Listing 3.29 return different values from the first?
questions.answer: Because NumPy keeps a hidden piece of global random state that advances with each call.
questions.explanation: The book: 'it's a hidden piece of global state', retrievable with np.random.get_state() and settable with np.random.seed(seed).

questions.question: Why can't JAX simply copy NumPy's random API, and what must a stateless version do instead?
questions.answer: JAX is stateless and cannot rely on hidden global state; the same API call must always return the same value, so random functions must take a seed argument and you pass different seeds to get different values.
questions.explanation: Final paragraph of the page, building on p.106.

questions.question: What does `jnp.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")` print?
questions.answer: Array([1., 2., 3.], dtype=float32)
questions.explanation: Last line of Listing 3.28.

questions.question: Which NumPy function sets the global random state?
questions.answer: np.random.seed(seed)
questions.explanation: get_state() retrieves the state, normal() samples (and advances it), and jnp.random.seed is not a JAX function — JAX uses keys (p.108).

questions.question: Name the two gradient utilities JAX provides according to the 3.5.1 list, and contrast them with how PyTorch exposes gradients.
questions.answer: jax.grad and jax.value_and_grad. PyTorch stores gradients on tensors via loss.backward() and .grad; JAX returns them from transformed functions.
questions.explanation: The list names the two utilities; the contrast uses pp.101-104 and the stateless idea from p.106 (the JAX details are on p.112).

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why jnp's default dtype being float32 and JAX arrays being immutable are both consistent with this page's description of JAX?
questions.answer: Immutability follows from the stateless design (no in-place state changes, hence the 'array assignment' difference); float32 is visible in Listing 3.28's outputs. (The default-dtype reason is beyond the book.)
questions.explanation: Self-check linking the printed outputs and the differences list to statelessness.

questions.question: You run `k = jax.random.key(123)` and then call `jax.random.normal(k, shape=(3,))` twice. What happens?
options: The second call returns different values because the key advanced
Both calls return exactly the same array
The second call raises an error because the key was consumed
The values differ unless you call np.random.seed(123) first
questions.answer: Both calls return exactly the same array
questions.explanation: Listing 3.30 shows both calls returning `[-0.1470326, 0.5524756, 1.648498]`. Keys are not advanced or consumed (options 1 and 3 are wrong), and NumPy's seed has no effect on JAX's PRNG (option 4 is wrong).

questions.question: Where does the key go in the argument list of a JAX random function, and why did JAX choose this design?
questions.answer: It is the first positional argument of every PRNG-using operation, which forces you to always provide a seed key.
questions.explanation: The page states that all JAX PRNG operations take `key` as their first positional argument 'to force you to always provide a seed key', since there is no global state to fall back on.

questions.question: In the NumPy `apply_noise` example, what is the role of `seed += 1`, and what is its JAX equivalent?
questions.answer: It gives the second call a different seed so `z` gets different noise from `y`; the caller manages seed state outside the function. In JAX you would derive a new key with `jax.random.split()` instead of incrementing an integer.
questions.explanation: The page says you must 'manage your seed state outside of the target function', and then introduces `jax.random.split()` as the way to create a new key from an existing one.

questions.question: What does `jax.random.key(1337)` return?
options: A random float drawn from a normal distribution
A special array structure (a key) that holds PRNG state
questions.answer: A special array structure (a key) that holds PRNG state
questions.explanation: The book: 'JAX doesn't use integer seeds. It uses special array structures called keys. You can create one from an integer value.' It is not the integer itself, not a sample, and not a NumPy object.

questions.question: Why is `jax.random.split()` being deterministic a desirable property rather than a limitation?
questions.answer: Because the whole program's randomness becomes reproducible from one root seed: the same sequence of splits always yields the same keys, so runs can be repeated exactly, while the new keys still give different values from the parent.
questions.explanation: The page notes that the same sequence of splits always results in the same final key; p.109 adds that statelessness maintains determinism, i.e., running the same code twice gives the same results.

questions.question: Beyond the book: what does `np.random.normal((3,))` in the `apply_noise` example actually compute, and how would you request three standard-normal samples?
questions.answer: `(3,)` is taken as `loc` (mean), so it returns one sample with mean 3, shape (1,). Use `np.random.normal(size=(3,))`.
questions.explanation: NumPy's signature is `normal(loc=0.0, scale=1.0, size=None)`; the first positional argument is the mean. The example's intent is clear either way, but the size keyword is needed for a shape.

questions.question: Can you write, from memory, code that creates a JAX key, splits it into two subkeys, and draws two different 3-element normal arrays?
questions.answer: `key = jax.random.key(0); k1, k2 = jax.random.split(key); a = jax.random.normal(k1, shape=(3,)); b = jax.random.normal(k2, shape=(3,))`
questions.explanation: This combines the three API pieces from this page: `key()`, key-first `normal()`, and `split()`. If `a` and `b` came out equal, you reused a key.

questions.question: What does `jax.random.split(seed_key, num=1)[0]` produce?
options: A single new key derived deterministically from `seed_key`
A new key that differs on every run of the program
questions.answer: A single new key derived deterministically from `seed_key`
questions.explanation: `split` returns an array of `num` new keys; `[0]` takes the one key. It differs from the parent (sampling gives new values) but is deterministic, so it is the same on every run. It is a key, not a float.

questions.question: Which two benefits of statelessness do the authors give to justify the extra work of managing keys?
questions.answer: Vectorizability (the compiler can automatically turn the code into highly parallel code) and determinism (running the same code twice gives the same results).
questions.explanation: Stated directly on the page, which adds that achieving both is impossible with a global PRNG state.

questions.question: After `x = jnp.array([1, 2, 3], dtype="float32")` and `new_x = x.at[0].set(10)`, what is `x`?
options: An error is raised at the second line
questions.explanation: `.at[].set()` creates a new tensor; `x` is not modified because JAX arrays are not assignable in place. `[10., 2., 3.]` is `new_x`, not `x`. No error occurs since this is the sanctioned API.

questions.question: Compute the final value of `e` in Listing 3.32.
questions.explanation: `b = c = ones`, `d = 2`s; `matmul(a, b)` sums two products of 1, giving 2 in every entry; `e *= d` multiplies element-wise by 2, giving 4s.

questions.question: Why does JAX forbid in-place assignment such as `x[0] = 10`?
questions.answer: Because any in-place modification would go against JAX's stateless design: functions must not change existing values, only produce new ones.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly and compares it to TensorFlow, whose tensors are also not assignable.

questions.question: In Listing 3.32, which line performs a matrix product rather than an element-wise operation?
questions.answer: e = jnp.matmul(a, b)
questions.explanation: The callout says `matmul` 'takes the product of two tensors (see chapter 2)'. The others are annotated as element-wise: square, addition and multiplication.

questions.question: Can you rewrite the NumPy snippet `x = np.zeros(3); x[1] = 5; x[2] += 1` in JAX without in-place assignment?
questions.answer: `x = jnp.zeros(3); x = x.at[1].set(5); x = x.at[2].add(1)`
questions.explanation: Each step creates a new array and rebinds `x`. `.set` is on this page; `.add` is part of the same `.at[]` API (beyond the book).

questions.question: What does `jax.grad(compute_loss)` return?
options: The gradient of the loss at the current parameters
The loss value and its gradient as a tuple
A new function that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to its first argument
questions.answer: A new function that computes the gradient of the loss with respect to its first argument
questions.explanation: JAX uses metaprogramming: functions that return functions. No values are computed yet (option 1). The tuple behaviour belongs to `jax.value_and_grad` (p.111). GradientTape is TensorFlow's mechanism.

questions.question: List the two properties a loss function must satisfy to be used with `jax.grad`.
questions.answer: It must return a scalar loss value, and its first argument must contain the state arrays you need gradients for.
questions.explanation: These are the two bullets on the page; the first argument is usually named `state` and can be an array, list or dict of arrays.

questions.question: For `compute_loss(input_var) = jnp.square(input_var)`, what does `grad_fn(-2.0)` return?
questions.explanation: The derivative of $x^2$ is $2x$; at $x=-2$ that is $-4$. (Hand calculation; the book's own call is on p.111.)

questions.question: Why is it natural that JAX, a stateless framework, computes gradients by transforming functions rather than by recording operations on stateful objects?
questions.answer: Because all relevant state is an explicit function argument, JAX can analyse the function itself and produce a new function giving gradients with respect to that argument; there are no hidden variables to track.
questions.explanation: This is an inference connecting the page's metaprogramming approach with the stateless design from p.106 and the requirement that the state be the first argument.

questions.question: In `dense(inputs, W, b)`, which operation applies the nonlinearity?
questions.answer: jax.nn.relu
questions.explanation: ReLU is the nonlinearity; `matmul` and `+ b` form the affine part. The function definition just packages the computation.

questions.question: If `state` is a dict `{"W": W, "b": b}`, what structure will `grad_fn(state, ...)` return?
questions.answer: A dict with the same keys, `{"W": dL/dW, "b": dL/db}`, each gradient having the shape of the corresponding array.
questions.explanation: The page says grad_fn returns gradient arrays corresponding to the first argument; with a single array it returns one array, so with a dict it returns a matching dict (the mirroring of structure is made explicit on p.111).

questions.question: Can you explain the three-step JAX gradient process to someone who knows only PyTorch, pointing out what replaces `loss.backward()`?
questions.answer: Write the loss as a function of the parameters, transform it once with `jax.grad`, then call the resulting function with the parameters; that call replaces `loss.backward()` + reading `.grad`.
questions.explanation: Check yourself against the numbered list on the page and the comparison with TensorFlow/PyTorch in the first paragraph.

questions.question: What does `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)` return when called as `grad_fn(state, x, y)`?
options: Only the gradients with respect to state
A tuple (loss, gradients with respect to state)
Gradients with respect to state, x and y
questions.answer: A tuple (loss, gradients with respect to state)
questions.explanation: value_and_grad returns the loss value first and the gradient(s) second. Plain `jax.grad` returns only gradients; the order is not reversed; and only the first argument is differentiated.

questions.question: Why would you use `jax.value_and_grad` instead of `jax.grad` plus a separate call to `compute_loss`?
questions.answer: Because you usually need the loss value too, and recomputing it independently outside grad_fn would be inefficient.
questions.explanation: Stated in 'Returning the loss value'; the forward pass needed for the gradient already produces the loss.

questions.question: If `state = {"W": W, "b": b}`, describe the structure of `grads_of_loss_wrt_state`.
questions.answer: A dict with keys "W" and "b", containing dL/dW (same shape as W) and dL/db (same shape as b).
questions.explanation: The page's callout says the gradients have the same structure as state, and state may be a dict or any tree.

questions.question: For `compute_loss(x) = x**2` and `grad_fn = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)`, what does `grad_fn(jnp.array(3.0))` return?
questions.explanation: Value $3^2 = 9$, gradient $2 \cdot 3 = 6$; value first, gradient second.

questions.question: In JAX parlance, what is a 'tree'?
options: A nested structure of tuples, dicts and lists
The computation graph recorded by a GradientTape
A binary tree of PRNG keys produced by split
questions.answer: A nested structure of tuples, dicts and lists
questions.explanation: Defined on this page. The other options are unrelated concepts: a model type, TensorFlow's tape, and a misreading of key splitting.

questions.question: What problem does `has_aux` solve?
questions.answer: Returning an extra by-product (e.g. the model `output`) from compute_loss alongside the loss, while JAX differentiates only the loss.
questions.explanation: The page motivates it as getting out 'an additional value output that's computed as a by-product of the loss computation'; the gradient function otherwise requires a scalar return value (p.110). The mechanics are on p.112.

questions.question: Can you write a `compute_loss(state, x, y)` for a linear model `pred = W*x + b` with MSE, wrap it in `value_and_grad`, and unpack loss and gradients?
questions.answer: `def compute_loss(state, x, y): W, b = state; return jnp.mean((W*x + b - y)**2)`; `loss, (dW, db) = jax.value_and_grad(compute_loss)((W, b), x, y)`
questions.explanation: Compare with the template on this page and with the classifier on p.112-113.

questions.question: Which two changes are needed to return an auxiliary output from a JAX loss function?
options: Return a dict and call jax.grad twice
Return a tuple (loss, extra output) and pass has_aux=True to value_and_grad()
Decorate the loss with @jax.jit and return the output first
Store the output in a global variable before returning the loss
questions.answer: Return a tuple (loss, extra output) and pass has_aux=True to value_and_grad()
questions.explanation: That is the two-step recipe on this page. jit is unrelated; returning the output first would make it the differentiated value; a global variable violates statelessness.

questions.question: Which TensorFlow decorator does the book say `@jax.jit` behaves identically to?
questions.answer: `@tf.function(jit_compile=True)`
questions.explanation: Stated directly; both compile the function with XLA.

questions.question: Why can only stateless functions be decorated with `@jax.jit`?
questions.answer: Because the compiled code only captures what flows in through arguments and out through return values; hidden state changes would not be reproduced, so any updated tensors must be returned.
questions.explanation: The book states the rule; the tracing explanation is beyond the book (see the 'What jit sees' note).

questions.question: In the pure-JAX linear classifier, how are `W` and `b` handled?
options: As tf.Variable objects updated with assign_sub
As attributes of a Keras layer
As function arguments, with new values returned by the function
As global arrays modified in place
questions.answer: As function arguments, with new values returned by the function
questions.explanation: The first bullet of 3.5.4. tf.Variable is TensorFlow's approach; Keras layers come later; in-place global modification is impossible in JAX.

questions.question: According to the JAX API, what is the structure returned by `jax.value_and_grad(f, has_aux=True)(...)`, and how does it compare with the book's unpacking?
questions.answer: `((loss, aux), grads)`; the book writes `loss, (grads, output)`, which nests the other way.
questions.explanation: This comes from the JAX documentation, not the book; it is flagged as a possible erratum. Use `(loss, output), grads = grad_fn(state, x, y)`.

questions.question: Name the two major differences between the JAX classifier and the TensorFlow/PyTorch versions.
questions.answer: All functions are stateless (W and b passed in, new values returned), and gradients are computed with `value_and_grad()`.
questions.explanation: Listed as the two bullets at the start of section 3.5.4.

questions.question: Could you explain to a colleague why the authors say this page is 'about as hard as JAX gets'?
questions.answer: Because it combines all the gradient plumbing: state as first argument, trees, value_and_grad, has_aux with nested tuples, plus the stateless requirement for jit.
questions.explanation: Revisit p.110-112 if any of these pieces is unclear.

questions.question: Why does `training_step` return `W` and `b` in addition to the loss?
options: Because the function is stateless, so the updated values are only available to the caller if returned
Because jax.jit requires every function to return three values
Because value_and_grad needs them for the next call
questions.answer: Because the function is stateless, so the updated values are only available to the caller if returned
questions.explanation: The page says the step must be stateless and must return the updated W and b. It is not just logging, jit does not impose a return count, and value_and_grad gets W and b as arguments from the caller.

questions.question: What is `state` in `compute_loss(state, inputs, targets)`, and why is it the first argument?
questions.answer: The tuple `(W, b)`; it is first because jax.value_and_grad differentiates with respect to the first argument, and we need gradients for W and b.
questions.explanation: The page describes state as 'a tuple of all the tensors we need gradients for'.

questions.question: With learning_rate = 0.1, b = [0.3] and grad_wrt_b = [-0.5], what is the new b?
questions.explanation: $b' = 0.3 - 0.1 \times (-0.5) = 0.35$; a negative gradient increases the parameter.
